title: SDISC: A Spike-Driven Human-Machine Interface with In-Situ Computing for Real-Time Low-Power Interaction
problem: Bio-signal processing for HMI (EMG, EEG) incurs high latency and power using conventional hardware; frame-based methods cannot achieve real-time energy-efficient edge inference.
motivation: Neuromorphic systems promise ultra-low-power inference; direct integration of spike-driven encoding and in-memory computing enables real-time HMI.
method: The system extracts features from bio-signals using spikes—brief pulses that capture meaningful activity while reducing data by over 10-fold compared to traditional frame-based methods. These spikes are computed directly inside RRAM (resistive memory, hardware that stores and processes data in one location), achieving high efficiency at 4.09 trillion operations per watt. To maintain accuracy despite RRAM's gradual performance changes and imperfections, the system uses two techniques: Spike-Activity-Distillation (identifying the most important computations) and Aid-Loser-Only (selectively reinforcing weaker memory cells).
key_novelty: Use spike-driven feature extraction from bio-signals processed directly in resistive memory (RRAM), with algorithms that compensate for the hardware's physical degradation over years of use to maintain accuracy.
contributions: 98% accuracy over 15+ days, 34 µs latency, 39.72 µW/sample
limitations: Evaluation limited to EMG-based control; generalization to other bio-signals (EEG, EOG) and multi-modal sensing not discussed.
